Photograph: Vlad Smilianets/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: ‘Shameful’ – Zelenskyy furious after shootout between Kyiv’s spy services Only shoot at Russian occupiers, president says, after three officers wounded in clash; Patriots could take years to make, says Rubio. What we know on day 1,653 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Wed 2 Sep 2026 21.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Volodymyr Zelenskyy blasted Ukraine’s SBU and GUR after a shootout in Kyiv between the two intelligence and security services reportedly left three officers injured. The SBU is Ukraine’s internal security service, like MI5 or the FBI. The GUR, or HUR, is its armed forces counterpart and also carries out military activities and special operations. Reports said the gunfight stemmed from the SBU taking into custody a leader of an anti-Kremlin Russian unit that fights for Ukraine under the watch of the GUR. Ukraine’s president called the situation “absolutely shameful” as he called in prosecutors and investigators, as well as firing a senior SBU officer. “Here in Ukraine, shooting is only permissible at Russian occupiers in defence of Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. “Our state will not perceive any other shootout as something that anyone is allowed to do.” Russian drones hit central Kyiv on Wednesday in a seventh ⁠day of intense strikes on the capital. Explosions were heard again in the early hours of Thursday morning. On Wednesday, 11 people were wounded, and residential and ⁠university buildings damaged. Russia also struck power facilities in the southern Odesa region with missiles and drones, authorities said, knocking out power to more than 350,000 homes. Two people were killed and eight wounded in strikes on the south-eastern city of Dnipro, the regional governor said, where food warehouses and educational buildings were damaged. Norway has seized ⁠a Russian cruise ship over unpaid compensation for the illegal annexation of Crimea. In April ⁠2023 a tribunal in The Hague ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.22bn to compensate for its Crimean assets that were seized when Moscow’s forces invaded. Naftogaz is a Ukrainian state oil and gas firm. Russia has refused to pay the compensation. Naftogaz said the seizure was ordered by the ‌Nord-Troms and Senja district court on 31 August. It said the vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was owned by Russia and used for commercial expedition cruises, including to the Norwegian archipelago Svalbard. Ukraine has urged the UN’s aviation agency, the ICAO, and its member countries ⁠to ban their airlines from Russian airspace , ​a day after Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned it was “becoming completely unsafe” because of Ukrainian drones . Ukraine wrote to agency seeking “the full prohibition by ICAO member states of civil aircraft operations within the airspace of the Russian Federation”. In response to Ukraine’s warning, the ICAO called on its members to ensure the safety of civilian aircraft. “Long-range weapons systems, unmanned aircraft systems [UAS], global navigation satellite system radio frequency interference, and advanced air defence systems are among the military technologies jeopardising civilian aviation.” Russian airspace becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, Zelenskyy says Read more It could take Ukraine several years to start building Patriot air defence interceptors and doing so is not an immediate solution for Kyiv, Marco Rubio has said. “I mean, these are highly sophisticated weaponry,” the US secretary of state told Fox News. The US was negotiating with Ukraine over licensed production of Patriot missiles, Rubio said. “That may come to fruition, but it really won’t solve the short-term challenge that they’re pointing to,” he said, adding that “the whole world is asking for more air interceptors” but US needs came first. “It’s become the number one defence need on the planet, not just for Ukraine, but on the planet,” including in the Middle East because of the US-Israeli war against Iran. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s air raid alerting system would be revised into two tiers – red for missiles, yellow for drones – allowing for more “predictability and a better understanding of how to react”. He added that curfew ⁠hours would be reduced and more above-ground transport options offered to compensate for metro closures. The measures were a response to “Russia’s changing tactics” and “its use of drones to wear down civilian life in our cities and disrupt normal economic activity across our country”, Zelenskyy said. Belgium has continued to block EU attempts to use €200bn in frozen Russian assets for Ukraine’s benefit. Opposition from Belgium has forced EU members to instead give Ukraine a €90bn loan off their own backs – but as that fund runs down, four countries have pushed to reopen the debate on the Russian assets. Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, said the Belgian government’s position remained “unchanged … Using these assets through a process akin to confiscation carries significant risk.” The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said after ministerial talks in Ireland that fresh funds for Ukraine should ultimately come from Russia. “That is why some of the member states were proposing to go back to the discussion of the frozen assets. And we will continue that discussion.” Britain’s sanctions enforcer, the OFSI, has fined Citibank £4.7m (US$6.35m) for failings and errors that led to banned Russians getting access to funds. Most of it happened between February and November 2022, the OFSI said. The CBNA London branch processed 970 payments totalling £19.7m – some for state-owned shipping company PJSC ‌Sovcomflot, as well as Alfa-Bank, PJSC Gazprombank and Credit Bank of Moscow. The agency did not consider there to ​have been any intent by CBNA London to breach sanctions, and the bank voluntarily disclosed most of the breaches. A Citi spokesperson said it ‌welcomed the conclusion of the ‌case and took sanctions compliance seriously. József Váradi, CEO of the Hungarian ultra-low-cost carrier, has publicly made the proposal, calling the loss-making state airline a waste of money and arguing that Romania does not need to subsidise it. Wizz Air, which commands a 51.3pc market share in Romania, has proposed managing these internal operations to improve efficiency and reduce the strain on Romanian taxpayers. See also NTSB reveals Air Boeing 767 crew attempted go-around before over-running Miami runway TAROM has explicitly rejected the offer, categorising Wizz Air’s pitch as completely unrealistic and unfeasible for a national carrier. This friction follows years of legal battles, with Wizz Air repeatedly challenging the European Commission’s approval of millions in state aid subsidies intended to keep TAROM afloat. European courts have continually dismissed Wizz Air’s appeals, with the European Court of Justice previously ruling that TAROM’s regional connectivity represents a critical public infrastructure that point-to-point budget airlines cannot easily replicate. Wizz Air has continued to expand aggressively across 14 Romanian airports, even as TAROM has defended its traditional hub-and-spoke domestic monopoly connecting regional cities to Bucharest. The airline’s proposal has come as TAROM continues to operate loss-making domestic routes that are considered essential for regional connectivity, with the Romanian Government maintaining its support for the national carrier despite ongoing financial challenges.
